title: the line
hook: everyone knows the scene where Lakshmana draws a line around the hut; Valmiki tells it differently
carry: let the forest be my witness

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's arrow struck the deer, and Maricha died crying out in Rama's voice. A voice in the wrong mouth.

In the version told on television and at bedtime, this is the moment of the line. Lakshmana, forced to leave, takes his arrow and draws a line in the earth around the hut. Don't cross it, he tells Sita, and nothing can harm you. The image is so familiar it has a name of its own. But open Valmiki's Ramayana here, read the scene line by line, and there is no line.
screen: `THE LINE IN THE EARTH.` → `DRAWN WITH AN ARROW.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's what Valmiki does tell. The cry reaches the hut: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! Sita hears Rama's voice in pain, and she's terrified. Go, she tells Lakshmana. Your brother is calling for help. Lakshmana doesn't move. He's sure of two things: no one in the three worlds can defeat Rama, and Rama told him not to leave her. That voice, he says, is a rakshasa's trick. And Sita, frightened out of her mind, says terrible things. You want him to die. You followed us into the forest because you want me. Or you're working for Bharata. She says she will die before she lets anyone but Rama touch her. These are words of fear, and the text doesn't pretend otherwise. Lakshmana is shattered. Your words are like burning iron in my ears, he says. You are like a goddess to me; I can't answer you. Then he says this: let the spirits of this forest be my witnesses. May they protect you. That's the guard he leaves: not a line in the dust, but a call to the forest itself, and his own grief at being doubted. He bows and goes, looking back again and again. Where the line came from is tomorrow's story. Today is Valmiki's version: two people who love Rama, both terrified for him, and the trick working through their fear.
screen: `SITA: GO, HE'S CALLING YOU.` · `LAKSHMANA: NO ONE CAN DEFEAT HIM.` · `WORDS OF FEAR.` · `LET THE FOREST BE MY WITNESS.` · then, large: `THE TRICK WORKS THROUGH FEAR.`

segments.voice: Think of a time someone you love said something harsh because they were frightened, or a time you did. Without replaying every word, notice that the fear came first and the words came after. If it feels right, let a little forgiveness move toward them, or toward yourself.
The line. In Valmiki, Lakshmana draws no line. He leaves Sita in the care of the forest spirits, after her frightened words have cut him deeply.
Your line: let the forest be my witness. Tomorrow, where the line came from. That's day five hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Reciters of Valmiki's Ramayana who pause on Sita's harsh words to Lakshmana explain them as words of terror for Rama, and Valmiki's Lakshmana leaves her in the care of the forest deities.

original.note: Sanskrit vanadevatā: the deities or spirits of the forest, whom Lakshmana calls on to guard Sita.

trapdoor: what you thought: Lakshmana drew a line and Sita stepped over it.
what it means: in Valmiki there's no line; Lakshmana leaves her with the forest spirits.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 45 has Sita's accusation and Lakshmana's appeal to the vanadevatas; the line enters the story in later tellings.

chat.says: Didn't Lakshmana draw a magic line around Sita before he left?
options: Not in Valmiki. There he asks the forest spirits to guard her; the line comes from later tellings.
Yes, Valmiki describes him drawing a glowing line around the hut with his arrow.
No, Lakshmana never left Sita alone at all; he stayed at the hut until Rama came home.
chat.meaning: In Valmiki, Lakshmana draws no line. Hurt by Sita's frightened words, he leaves her in the care of the forest spirits.

Valmiki.meaning: the poet traditionally credited with the Sanskrit Ramayana

Ramayana.meaning: the epic of Rama, his exile, and the rescue of Sita

rakshasa.meaning: a demon-like being of the forest and of Lanka
